items.stem: What is science?

options.label: A
options.text: A method of memorizing facts and figures about the universe

options.label: B
options.text: A process of conducting experiments without any specific questions

options.label: C
options.text: A way of thinking, observing, and doing things to understand the world

options.label: D
options.text: A collection of beliefs about how things work

items.answer: (C) A way of thinking, observing, and doing things to understand the world. Science is a systematic approach involving curiosity, questioning, exploration, and experimentation to understand the natural world and the universe. It is a dynamic process of discovery rather than a static set of facts.

items.stem: Why is science described as a “giant and unending jigsaw puzzle”?

options.label: A
options.text: Because it is a game that only a few can play

options.label: B
options.text: Because new discoveries add pieces, leading to more questions

options.label: C
options.text: Because it has a fixed number of pieces to be discovered

options.label: D
options.text: Because it is primarily about solving complex mathematical problems

items.answer: (B) Because new discoveries add pieces, leading to more questions. Science is likened to an unending jigsaw puzzle because each new finding or discovery provides a piece of understanding, which in turn opens up new questions and areas for further exploration, making the process continuous.

items.stem: What is the scientific method?

options.label: A
options.text: A rigid set of rules that must be followed in a specific order

options.label: B
options.text: A way to prove pre-existing beliefs about the natural world

options.label: C
options.text: A step-by-step process of observing, questioning, guessing, and testing

options.label: D
options.text: A method used exclusively by professional scientists in laboratories

items.answer: (C) A step-by-step process of observing, questioning, guessing, and testing. The scientific method is a systematic approach to investigation that involves making observations, formulating questions, making educated guesses (hypotheses), and then testing these guesses through experiments or further observations to arrive at conclusions.

items.stem: A student notices that plants kept in a dark room do not grow well. Using the scientific method, what would be their next logical step after this observation?

options.label: A
options.text: Immediately conclude that all plants need sunlight

options.label: B
options.text: Ask a question, such as “Does sunlight affect plant growth?”

options.label: C
options.text: Conduct an experiment by giving some plants extra fertilizer

options.label: D
options.text: Ignore the observation as it might be a coincidence

items.answer: (B) Ask a question, such as “Does sunlight affect plant growth?” After making an observation (plants in a dark room not growing well), the next step in the scientific method is to formulate a question based on that observation to guide further investigation.

items.stem: Why is it said that anyone using the scientific method is acting like a scientist?

options.label: A
options.text: Because only professional scientists use the scientific method

options.label: B
options.text: Because the scientific method is about common sense, which everyone possesses

options.label: C
options.text: Because everyday problem-solving often involves observing, guessing, and testing

options.label: D
options.text: Because scientists are the only ones who ask questions about the world

items.answer: (C) Because everyday problem-solving often involves observing, guessing, and testing. The basic principles of the scientific method—like observing, asking questions, forming hypotheses, and testing them—are often used in everyday situations, such as finding out why a pen has stopped working or why food spilled from a cooker.

items.stem: How is science different from just memorizing facts?

options.label: A
options.text: Memorizing facts is more important in science than the process of discovery

options.label: B
options.text: Science is a dynamic process of inquiry, while memorizing is passive

options.label: C
options.text: True science does not involve any memorization of facts at all

options.label: D
options.text: Memorizing facts is the first step of the scientific method

items.answer: (B) Science is a dynamic process of inquiry, while memorizing is passive. Science involves actively thinking, observing, and experimenting to understand how things work, rather than simply memorizing facts and figures.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT considered a step in the scientific method?

options.label: A
options.text: Observing something that is interesting

options.label: B
options.text: Guessing a possible answer to a question

options.label: C
options.text: Accepting a guess without testing it

options.label: D
options.text: Testing a guess through experiments or more observations

items.answer: (C) Accepting a guess without testing it. The scientific method involves testing guesses (hypotheses) through experiments or further observations. Accepting a guess without any form of testing goes against the principles of scientific inquiry.

items.stem: Imagine you are trying to figure out why your flashlight isn’t working. First, you observe it’s not turning on. You guess the batteries might be dead. You then replace the batteries. According to the scientific method described, what is your action of replacing the batteries an example of?

options.label: A
options.text: Making an initial observation

options.label: B
options.text: Forming a question

options.label: C
options.text: Testing your guess (hypothesis)

options.label: D
options.text: Analyzing the results

items.answer: (C) Testing your guess (hypothesis). In this scenario, observing the flashlight not working is the initial observation. Guessing the batteries are dead is forming a hypothesis. The act of replacing the batteries is the step of testing that hypothesis to see if it resolves the problem.

items.stem: What does the idea that “new discoveries often change our understanding of the world” suggest about scientific knowledge?

options.label: A
options.text: Scientific knowledge is absolute and never changes

options.label: B
options.text: Scientific knowledge can evolve and be revised based on new evidence

options.label: C
options.text: Old scientific discoveries are always incorrect and should be discarded

options.label: D
options.text: Understanding the world is not possible through science

items.answer: (B) Scientific knowledge can evolve and be revised based on new evidence. This statement highlights that science is a progressive field. As new evidence emerges and new discoveries are made, existing scientific understanding can be refined, modified, or even overturned, reflecting the dynamic nature of scientific knowledge.

items.stem: What is a key benefit of working together with friends in science?

options.label: A
options.text: It makes experiments less accurate

options.label: B
options.text: It is always more fun to discover things together

options.label: C
options.text: It helps in memorizing facts more easily

options.label: D
options.text: It eliminates the need for individual curiosity

items.answer: (B) It is always more fun to discover things together. Collaborative learning in science makes discovery more enjoyable, and reflects how scientists often work together in teams to solve problems and share ideas.

items.stem: What is the term for a guess or a possible answer to a scientific question before it is tested?

options.label: A
options.text: A theory

options.label: B
options.text: A law

options.label: C
options.text: A hypothesis

options.label: D
options.text: An observation

items.answer: (C) A hypothesis In the scientific method, a hypothesis is an educated guess or a proposed explanation for an observation, which is then tested through experimentation or further observation to determine its validity.

items.stem: What does the phrase “To be a wise person, you must be a ‘whys’ person!” emphasize about learning science?

options.label: A
options.text: Memorizing answers to all “why” questions

options.label: B
options.text: Constantly asking questions and seeking understanding

options.label: C
options.text: Believing everything you are told without questioning

options.label: D
options.text: Avoiding difficult questions in science

items.answer: (B) Constantly asking questions and seeking understanding. This phrase encourages a curious and inquisitive mindset, highlighting that the path to wisdom and scientific understanding involves consistently asking “why” and seeking deeper explanations for phenomena observed in the world.

items.stem: If a student observes that a particular type of bird is only seen during winter in their area, what scientific question could arise from this observation?

options.label: A
options.text: Are all birds migratory?

options.label: B
options.text: Why does this bird species appear only in winter?

options.label: C
options.text: What is the bird’s favorite food?

options.label: D
options.text: How many feathers does this bird have?

items.answer: (B) Why does this bird species appear only in winter? The observation of a bird appearing seasonally would naturally lead to a question about the reason for this specific pattern, such as investigating its migratory behavior or seasonal adaptations.

items.stem: Where can science be found in our daily lives?

options.label: A
options.text: Only in laboratories and research institutions

options.label: B
options.text: Only in textbooks and scientific journals

options.label: C
options.text: Everywhere, from the depths of the ocean to outer space

options.label: D
options.text: Only in complex natural phenomena, not everyday things

items.answer: (C) Everywhere, from the depths of the ocean to outer space. The explicitly states that “the most wonderful thing about science is that it is everywhere,” encompassing a vast range of scales and environments, from the microscopic to the cosmic, and including everyday occurrences.

items.stem: What does the idea of moving a puzzle piece in science refer to?

options.label: A
options.text: The idea that scientific experiments often fail

options.label: B
options.text: The self-correcting nature of science where existing ideas are revised with new evidence

options.label: C
options.text: The fact that scientists often misplace their equipment

options.label: D
options.text: The process of creating new scientific theories from scratch

items.answer: (B) The self-correcting nature of science where existing ideas are revised with new evidence. This analogy refers to the way scientific understanding evolves. When new data or better explanations emerge, previously accepted ideas or theories might be re-evaluated and modified, demonstrating science’s capacity to correct and refine itself.

items.stem: What is the primary aim of asking questions and exploring the world in science?

options.label: A
options.text: To prove personal opinions

options.label: B
options.text: To understand how things work and uncover secrets of the universe

options.label: C
options.text: To create complex technologies immediately

options.label: D
options.text: To find the simplest answers to all questions

items.answer: (B) To understand how things work and uncover secrets of the universe. Science is the pursuit of understanding how the world and the universe work, involving exploration, asking questions and discovering the principles of nature..

items.stem: The example of a bicycle repair person trying to find an air leak is used to illustrate:

options.label: A
options.text: That only mechanics use the scientific method

options.label: B
options.text: How complex scientific problems are solved

options.label: C
options.text: That everyday problem-solving can involve a scientific approach

options.label: D
options.text: The importance of having the right tools for science

items.answer: (C) That everyday problem-solving can involve a scientific approach. This example, along with others like a cook figuring out why dal spilled, is used to show that the systematic process of questioning, guessing, and testing (the scientific method) is not limited to formal science but is also applied in everyday problem-solving scenarios.

items.stem: What is the new subject introduced for exploring the world in the Middle Stage of school?
items.answer: Science

items.stem: What is the most important quality needed for science?
items.answer: Curiosity.

items.stem: What is the title of the Grade 6 Science textbook mentioned?
items.answer: Curiosity.

items.stem: Name one mystery of nature that science helps unravel.
items.answer: Why stars shine.

items.stem: Where can science be found, according to the text?
items.answer: Everywhere.

items.stem: Do new scientific discoveries ever lead to changes in our understanding?
items.answer: Yes

items.stem: Which planet is uniquely known to support life?
items.answer: Earth.

items.stem: Besides food, what essential substance do we need for survival mentioned in the text?
items.answer: Water.

items.stem: What happens to water when it is cooled sufficiently?
items.answer: It freezes and becomes ice.

items.stem: What is produced when water is heated sufficiently?
items.answer: It boils and becomes steam.

items.stem: What everyday object was used as an example for applying the scientific method when it stops working?
items.answer: A pen.

items.stem: What is the first step in the scientific method after observing something?
items.answer: Wonder and think of a question.

items.stem: What are people called who follow the scientific method to solve problems?
items.answer: Scientists

items.stem: Can a person be considered working like a scientist if they follow the scientific method in daily life?
items.answer: Yes.

items.stem: What is the foremost thing needed to learn science well?
items.answer: To be curious and observe surroundings keenly.

items.stem: When curiosity is sparked, what kinds of questions do we begin to ask?
items.answer: How and why.

items.stem: Is science typically an individual or a team effort?
items.answer: A team effort.

items.stem: What kind of “person” should you be to become a wise person?
items.answer: A “whys” person.

items.stem: Explain the meaning of “Science” .
items.answer: Science is a way of thinking, observing, and doing things to understand our world and uncover the universe’s secrets, like a grand adventure of inquiry.

items.stem: Why is the Grade 6 Science textbook titled “Curiosity”?
items.answer: The textbook is titled “Curiosity” because having curiosity is the most important thing needed to explore, ask questions, and understand how things work in science.

items.stem: List two examples of natural phenomena that suggests science helps us understand.
items.answer: Science helps us understand mysteries like why stars shine in the night sky and how a flower knows the precise moment to bloom.

items.stem: What interesting aspect of food in India does the chapter point out?
items.answer: The chapter points out that in a diverse country like India, food is fascinating, with different cuisines and many tasty dishes to explore.

items.stem: What are two questions about water that the chapter encourages readers to think about?
items.answer: The chapter encourages readers to wonder why and how it rains, and to notice how water changes form when cooled or heated.

items.stem: Name three different types of materials mentioned in the chapter that we use.
items.answer: The chapter mentions materials such as paper we write on, a metal key, a plastic ruler, a rubber eraser, magnets, and clothes.

items.stem: How does the chapter suggest we can expand our scientific inquiry beyond Earth?
items.answer: The chapter suggests expanding our inquiry by asking questions about celestial bodies like the Sun, the Moon, and the millions of stars in the sky.

items.stem: Briefly outline the problem-solving steps described for a pen that stops writing.
items.answer: If a pen stops writing, first guess the ink is finished and test by checking. If ink is present, guess it dried up and test differently.

items.stem: What are the three core actions of the scientific method after an observation and question?
items.answer: After observing and questioning, the core actions are: guess a possible (hypothesis), test this guess through experiments or observations, and analyze the results.

items.stem: Give an example from the chapter of someone applying scientific thinking in a daily task.
items.answer: An example is someone cooking who wonders why dal spilled from the cooker, questioning if too much water was used, thus applying scientific thinking.

items.stem: How does learning science, according to the chapter, improve our problem-solving abilities?
items.answer: Learning science develops our capabilities for finding solutions to bigger problems and solving more universal mysteries by understanding and applying the scientific method effectively.

items.stem: What does the chapter advise if you cannot find an answer to a question on your own?
items.answer: If you cannot find an alone, the chapter advises asking friends for help, as science is often a collaborative effort and discovery is more fun together.

items.stem: How is the journey of learning science portrayed in terms of duration in the chapter?
items.answer: The journey of learning science is portrayed as an ongoing exploration spanning several years, possibly extending beyond school, with continuous discoveries and new questions.

items.stem: What joyful activity is science compared to at the end of the chapter?
items.answer: At the end, science is compared to children joyfully enjoying the rain, emphasizing that science is fundamentally about joyful exploration and continuous wonder.

items.stem: What is the significance of being a “whys” person, as mentioned in the chapter’s conclusion?
items.answer: Being a “whys” person, someone who constantly asks ‘why’, is significant because this inquisitive nature is key to becoming a wise person through scientific exploration.

items.stem: What is the primary aim of the “Curiosity” textbook as suggested by the introductory chapter?
items.answer: The primary aim is to ignite students’ spirit of inquiry, encouraging them to explore their surroundings, ask questions, and understand the world using scientific principles.

items.stem: What examples of natural transformations does the chapter offer that can spark curiosity?
items.answer: The chapter offers transformations like a seed growing into a plant or a caterpillar changing into a beautiful butterfly as observations that can spark curiosity.

items.stem: The “Science” not just as a subject but as a “way of thinking.” Elaborate on this idea using details from the text, and explain why ‘Curiosity’ is deemed its most vital component.
items.answer: Science as a dynamic process of thinking, observing, and acting to comprehend our world and its mysteries. It’s an adventure of inquiry, not static knowledge. ‘Curiosity’ is vital because it’s the engine of this process. It’s the inherent urge to ask “why” and “how,” which fuels observation, questioning, exploration, and ultimately, the joy of discovery. The textbook itself is named “Curiosity” to emphasize its role in fostering this spirit, suggesting that true scientific engagement begins with a curious mind eager to explore and understand.

items.stem: Discuss the analogy “Science is like a giant and unending jigsaw puzzle”. How does this comparison explain the nature and progression of scientific knowledge?
items.answer: This analogy effectively portrays science as a vast, complex, and ever-expanding field of knowledge. Each new discovery is like adding a new piece to the puzzle, enhancing our understanding. The “unending” aspect highlights that science is never complete; each often uncovers more questions, leading to continuous investigation. It also implies that scientific knowledge is built progressively and collaboratively. Furthermore, the idea that pieces might be “put in the wrong place” reflects how scientific understanding can evolve, with new evidence correcting or refining previous theories and conclusions.

items.stem: “The most wonderful thing about science is that it is everywhere.” Justify this statement with at least four distinct examples provided in the chapter, covering different scales or environments.
items.answer: Science’s omnipresence with diverse examples. It’s in the vastness of outer space (stars shining), in natural processes (a flower blooming, a seed growing), in our homes (cooking in the kitchen, properties of water), and even in the materials we use daily (paper, plastic, metal). It ranges from studying microscopic grains of sand to massive mountains and from the depths of the ocean to our playgrounds. This pervasiveness shows that scientific principles and inquiry are applicable to understanding all aspects of our existence and environment, not just formal laboratory settings.

items.stem: Describe the scientific method using the everyday example of a pen that stops writing, as explained in the chapter. What are the general sequential steps involved in this method?
items.answer: When a pen stops writing, the scientific method begins with an observation and a question: “Why did it stop?” Then, a hypothesis is formed, e.g., “the ink finished.” This is tested by checking the refill. If the test fails (ink is present), a new hypothesis, like “the ink dried up,” is proposed and tested differently. The general steps are:

items.stem: How does the chapter encourage students to seek answers to their questions, and what role does collaboration play in the scientific process ?
items.answer: The chapter encourages students to pro-actively seek s by keenly observing, asking “how and why,” and applying the scientific method of guessing and testing. It stresses that this isn’t just for professional scientists. If an isn’t found individually, the text strongly advocates for collaboration, stating, “ask your friends to help you out!” It highlights that science is rarely a solitary pursuit; scientists worldwide work in teams, and discovering things together is portrayed as more effective and enjoyable, reflecting the collaborative nature of scientific advancement.

items.stem: What are some of the broad thematic areas of study hinted at in this introductory chapter that students will likely explore in the “Curiosity” textbook? Mention at least three.
items.answer: Firstly, students will explore Earth, its environment and the diversity of life, including how plants and animals grow. Secondly, they will delve into the science of everyday things, such as food, its composition, and different materials around us like paper, metal, and plastic. Thirdly, fundamental concepts like water and its properties, understanding temperature (hot and cold), and even extending curiosity to celestial bodies like the Sun, Moon, and stars will be part of their scientific journey.

items.stem: The scientific thinking is not confined to scientists alone but is applied in many daily life situations. Explain this with two distinct examples given in the text.
items.answer: A person cooking who wonders why dal spilled from the cooker, hypothesizing if there was too much water. This mirrors scientific questioning. Another example is a bicycle repair person trying to locate an air leak in a flat tyre, or an electrician determining why a bulb isn’t working by checking the bulb or switch. In both scenarios, individuals observe a problem, form a guess about the cause, and then investigate or test their guess, which is the essence of applying the scientific method in everyday problem-solving.

items.stem: Explain the chapter’s concluding message: “to be a wise person, you must be a ‘whys’ person!” What does this emphasize about learning and the scientific mindset?
items.answer: This concluding message powerfully emphasizes that wisdom is cultivated through persistent inquiry and a relentless desire to understand the underlying reasons for things – by constantly asking “why?” In the context of science, it reinforces that learning is an active process driven by curiosity, not passive memorization. Being a “whys” person signifies a commitment to questioning, investigating, and seeking explanations, which are the hallmarks of a scientific mindset. It suggests that true understanding and sagacity emerge from this inquisitive engagement with the world, promoting a lifelong habit of critical thinking and exploration.

items.stem: How does this first chapter aim to bridge the gap between students’ prior experiences in the Preparatory Stage and the formal introduction of Science in the Middle Stage?
items.answer: This chapter bridges the gap by acknowledging and validating students’ innate curiosity and exploratory experiences from the Preparatory Stage. It frames the formal introduction of Science in the Middle Stage not as a completely new or alien discipline, but as a continuation and enhancement of their natural desire to discover and understand. By emphasizing that science is an exciting journey fueled by asking questions— something children naturally do—it aims to make the transition smoother, fostering enthusiasm for the subject by connecting it to their inherent inquisitiveness.

items.stem: What perspective does the chapter offer regarding questions that might not be immediately answerable within Grade 6? How does it portray the nature of scientific learning over time?
items.answer: The chapter reassures students not to be disheartened if all their questions aren’t ed in Grade 6. It portrays scientific learning as a long-term, ongoing journey, stating they are “embarking upon a journey of science for the next five years or even beyond!” This perspective emphasizes that science is a process of continuous discovery rather than a collection of finite facts to be quickly memorized. It encourages sustained curiosity and patience, suggesting that deeper understanding unfolds progressively as they continue their exploration through their academic years and perhaps throughout their lives.

items.stem: Rohan observed that ice cubes melt faster when crushed into smaller pieces compared to a single large ice cube of the same total weight. He wondered why this happens, even though the amount of ice is the same. He thought it might have something to do with how much of the ice touches the warmer air. (i) What specific observation did Rohan make about melting ice? (ii) What was Rohan’s initial thought or hypothesis about why this occurs? (iii) Explain scientifically why crushed ice melts faster, relating to Rohan’s hypothesis. (iv) Suggest a simple way Rohan could visually compare the surface area of a whole ice cube versus crushed ice.
items.answer: (i) Rohan observed that crushed ice cubes melt faster than a single large ice cube of the same total weight. (ii) Rohan thought it might be related to how much of the ice surface is in contact with the warmer air. (iii) Crushing ice increases its total surface area exposed to the warmer surrounding air. More surface area means more contact points for heat transfer from the air to the ice, causing it to absorb heat and melt more quickly. (iv) Rohan could imagine dipping both in paint and then seeing how much area is painted; the crushed ice would show a much larger total painted area.

items.stem: During a school trip to a botanical garden, Priya noticed that some plants had labels indicating they “close their leaves at night.” That evening, she observed a plant in her own balcony whose leaves seemed to droop and fold inwards as it got dark. She wondered if this was a common behavior and why plants might do it. (i) What observation in the botanical garden and her balcony made Priya curious? (ii) What question did Priya’s observation lead her to ask? (iii) Suggest one possible reason why some plants might close their leaves at night. (iv) If Priya wanted to investigate further, what simple observation could she make over several days regarding her balcony plant and daylight?
items.answer: (i) Priya noticed plants that close their leaves at night in the garden and observed similar behavior in her balcony plant. (ii) Priya wondered if this leaf-closing behavior was common and why plants might do it. (iii) Closing leaves at night might help some plants conserve water by reducing surface area exposed to cooler night air, or it could be a way to protect against nocturnal herbivores or even conserve energy. (iv) Priya could observe her balcony plant at different times: sunrise, midday, sunset, and after dark for several days, noting the position of its leaves to see if there is a consistent pattern related to light.

items.stem: Ali was trying to dissolve sugar in three glasses of water: one with cold water, one with tap water (room temperature), and one with warm water. He used the same amount of sugar and water in each glass and stirred them equally. He noticed a difference in how quickly the sugar disappeared in each glass. (i) What was Ali trying to investigate with his three glasses of water and sugar? (ii) What difference did Ali likely observe regarding the sugar in the three glasses? (iii) Based on common scientific understanding, explain why this difference occurs. (iv) If Ali wanted to make his experiment more precise, what is one thing he should ensure is exactly the same for all three glasses, besides the amount of sugar and water?
items.answer: (i) Ali was trying to investigate how water temperature affects the speed at which sugar dissolves. (ii) Ali likely observed that the sugar dissolved fastest in the warm water, slower in the tap water, and slowest in the cold water. (iii) Sugar dissolves faster in warmer water because the water molecules have more energy and move more quickly, leading to more frequent collisions with sugar particles, breaking them apart and dispersing them faster. (iv) Ali should ensure that the stirring method (speed and duration) is exactly the same for all three glasses to ensure a fair comparison.

items.stem: While playing with a magnet, Sonia discovered that it attracted her steel hairpin but did not attract a copper coin or a plastic button. She tried it on various small objects around her house and started to group them based on whether they were attracted to the magnet or not. (i) What initial discovery did Sonia make with her magnet? (ii) What activity did Sonia engage in after her initial discovery? (iii) What property of materials was Sonia exploring through her activity? (iv) If Sonia found that an iron nail and a steel paperclip were attracted, but an aluminum foil piece was not, what could she conclude about aluminum compared to iron and steel?
items.answer: (i) Sonia discovered that her magnet attracted a steel hairpin but did not attract a copper coin or a plastic button. (ii) Sonia started testing the magnet on various small objects and began grouping them based on their attraction to the magnet. (iii) Sonia was exploring the magnetic property of materials, specifically identifying which materials are magnetic (attracted to a magnet) and which are non-magnetic. (iv) Sonia could conclude that aluminum is a non-magnetic material, unlike iron and steel, which are magnetic materials.

items.stem: A group of students was tasked with finding out how the length of a simple pendulum (a weight tied to a string) affects the time it takes to make one complete swing (its period). They made pendulums of different string lengths and timed 10 swings for each, then calculated the time for one swing. (i) What were the students investigating about a simple pendulum? (ii) What did they vary in their experiment, and what did they measure? (iii) Why was it a good idea for them to time 10 swings and then calculate the time for one swing, rather than just timing one swing? (iv) If they observed that longer pendulums took more time for one swing, what relationship would they be discovering?
items.answer: (i) The students were investigating how the length of a simple pendulum’s string affects the time it takes for one complete swing (its period). (ii) They varied the length of the pendulum string and measured the time taken for 10 swings (to then calculate the time for one swing). (iii) Timing 10 swings and then dividing by 10 reduces the impact of human reaction time errors in starting and stopping the timer, leading to a more accurate average time for a single swing. (iv) They would be discovering a direct relationship: as the length of the pendulum increases, the time period (time for one swing) also increases.

items.stem: Remove the seed coat of a chickpea. Now, observe the structure of the chickpea and maize seeds. Are they similar or different? Figure : Dicot and monocot seeds
items.answer: After soaking chickpea and maize seeds for two days, we observed them. Chickpea Seed: When we removed the seed coat of the chickpea, we found that the seed could be easily split into two equal halves. These two parts are the cotyledons. So, chickpea has two cotyledons. Maize Seed: The maize seed did not split into two parts like the chickpea. Even after soaking, it remained as a single piece. It has only one cotyledon. Similarities/Differences: They are different. The most obvious difference is that the chickpea seed has two cotyledons (it’s a dicot seed ), while the maize seed has only one cotyledon (it’s a monocot seed ). The chickpea seed is also more rounded, while the maize seed is flatter and somewhat shield-shaped. Activity 2.9 : Let us find out You have recorded the movement of a few animals in Table. You may have also observed how other animals move from place to place. Let us now think about the types of movement in animals. A number of animals are shown in Figure. You can add more animals that you may have observed and create a poster on the variety of animals. Which body parts are used by the animals in the poster you created and those in Figure for movement? Figure : Diversity in animals

items.stem: Share and discuss the basis of grouping you have made with other groups in your class. You will be surprised to see that the basis used by different groups may vary. What do you think are the reasons behind it? Different students might have chosen different common features for the grouping. For example, some students may have chosen the height of plants as the basis for grouping while others might have chosen presence or absence of flowers as the basis for grouping of plants (See Figure). Figure : Some possible criteria of groupings of plants and animals
items.answer: Our group collected about 30 picture cards of different plants and animals. For plants, one way we grouped them was: Plants that give flowers (e.g., rose, sunflower, hibiscus). Plants that do not give prominent flowers (or we couldn’t see them in the picture, e.g., ferns, moss, pine tree). Another way we grouped plants was by their size: Tall plants (e.g., coconut tree, mango tree). Medium-sized plants (e.g., lemon plant, rose bush). Small plants (e.g., grass, mint). For animals, one way we grouped them was by where they live: Animals that live on land (e.g., lion, elephant, dog). Animals that live in water (e.g., fish, dolphin, octopus). Animals that can fly (e.g., bird, bat, butterfly). Another way we grouped animals was by what they eat (based on our general knowledge): Animals that eat plants (e.g., cow, deer, rabbit). Animals that eat other animals (e.g., tiger, snake, eagle). When we discussed with other groups, we found they used different features for grouping. For plants, one group used “hard stem” vs “soft stem”. For animals, another group used “has fur” vs “has feathers” vs “has scales”. The reasons for these different groupings are that different groups chose different common features that they thought were important or easy to see in the pictures. There are many ways to group the same set of plants and animals depending on which characteristic you focus on. Activity 2.4 : Let us group

items.answer: (a) Wheat plant: It has fibrous roots (many thin roots arising from the stem-base) and its leaves show parallel venation (veins run side- by-side from base to tip). (b) Kidney-bean plant: It has a tap root (one main thick root with smaller side roots) and its leaves show reticulate venation (veins form a network pattern).

items.stem: Manu’s mother maintains a kitchen garden. One day, she was digging out radish from the soil. She told Manu that radish is a kind of root. Examine a radish and write what type of root it is. What type of venation would you observe in the leaves of radish plant?
items.answer: Radish is a tap root that has become thick and fleshy to store food. The leaves of the radish plant show reticulate venation, where the veins branch and form a network.

items.stem: Look at the image of a mountain goat and a goat found in the plains. Point out the similarities and differences between them. What are the reasons for these differences?
items.answer: Aspect Mountain Goat Plain-land Goat Reason Similarities Both are mammals, have four legs, cloven hooves and eat plants (herbivores). – These are common features of goats as a species. Body build Stocky body, shorter legs but very strong muscles. Comparati- vely slimmer body, normal leg strength. Strong, short legs give better balance on steep, rocky slopes. Feet / Hooves Hooves are harder and have rough pads for gripping rocks. Hooves are smoother— good for flat ground. Adaptation for sure footing on mountains.

items.stem: Look at the image of a mountain goat and a goat found in the plains. Point out the similarities and differences between them. What are the reasons for these differences? Ans : Aspect Mountain Goat Plain-land Goat Reason Similarities Both are mammals, have four legs, cloven hooves and eat plants (herbivores). – These are common features of goats as a species. Body build Stocky body, shorter legs but very strong muscles. Comparati- vely slimmer body, normal leg strength. Strong, short legs give better balance on steep, rocky slopes. Feet / Hooves Hooves are harder and have rough pads for gripping rocks. Hooves are smoother— good for flat ground. Adaptation for sure footing on mountains.
items.answer: Yes, when we looked at the fallen leaves we collected, we noticed a lot of variation. Shape and Structure: Some leaves were long and narrow (like grass), some were broad and somewhat round (like a lotus leaf, if we had one), some were heart-shaped, and some had toothed edges (like hibiscus or rose leaflets). Some leaves were small, others were large. Some were thick, and some were thin. Veins and Venation: We observed the thin lines called veins on the leaves. In the hibiscus leaf Figure (a), the veins form a net-like pattern on both sides of a main, thick middle vein. This is called reticulate venation. In the banana leaf Figure (b), the veins run parallel to each other. This is called parallel venation. The grass leaf Figure (c) also shows veins running parallel to each other, so it also has parallel venation. So, the main difference is that in reticulate venation, the veins branch out and form a network, while in parallel venation, they run alongside each other without forming a network. items.stem: After you are done observing, make sure to replant the herbs so that they may continue to thrive and grow. What are the similarities and differences in the roots of the plants collected by you? What differences do you see in the roots of plants shown in Figure (a) and Figure (b)? Figure : Types of roots
items.answer: We went to an open area and carefully dug out a small weed (like a common broadleaf weed) and some grass, making sure to wet the soil first so the roots wouldn’t break. We washed the roots with water. Similarities and Differences in Collected Roots: The roots of the weed had one main, thick root going downwards, with smaller, thinner roots coming out from its sides. The roots of the grass looked like a bunch of many thin, similar-sized roots spreading out from the base of the stem. A similarity is that all roots help to hold the plant in the soil. Differences were in their structure – one had a main root, the other had a bushy bunch. Differences in Figure (a) and Figure (b): In Figure (a) (mustard plant), there is one main, prominent root that goes deep into the soil, and smaller roots branch off from this main root. This is called a taproot. In Figure (b) (common grass), there is no single main root. Instead, there is a cluster or bunch of many thin, fibre-like roots that arise from the base of the stem. These are called fibrous roots. After observing, we carefully replanted the herbs. Activity 2.7 : Let us relate and analyse

items.stem: Earthworm Crawls Body segments, muscles, setae (bristles)
items.answer: Animals use different body parts for movement. Ant: Walks and crawls using its legs. Goat: Walks and jumps using its legs. Pigeon: Walks using its legs and flies using its wings. Housefly: Walks using its legs and flies using its wings. Fish: Swims using its fins. Snake (from Figure): Slithers or crawls using its whole body, with the help of muscles and scales. Frog (from Figure): Hops on land using its powerful hind legs and swims in water using its legs, often with webbed feet. Earthworm (from Figure): Crawls by alternately shortening and lengthening its body segments, using muscles and tiny bristles called setae. Butterfly (from Figure): Flies using its wings. Rabbit (from Figure): Hops and runs using its legs. Tortoise (from Figure): Walks slowly using its legs. Conclusions from Table: Different animals have different ways of moving, like walking, flying, swimming, crawling, hopping, etc. They use different body parts for these movements, such as legs, wings, fins, or even their whole body. items.stem: Scorpion Rhodo- dendron Sea turtle Elephant Frog
items.answer: Observations regarding plants and animals in various regions: The plants and animals found in one type of region are often very different from those found in another. In the desert: We listed Camel, Cactus, Date Palm, Desert Fox, and Scorpion. These are adapted to hot and dry conditions with little water. For example, cactus has fleshy stems to store water. Camels can survive long without water. On mountains: We listed Deodar tree, Mountain Goat, Pine tree, Yak, and Rhododendron. These are adapted to cold conditions, and sometimes snow and strong winds. Deodar trees are conical so snow slides off. Mountain goats have features for climbing. Rhododendrons on mountain tops might be shorter with smaller leaves. In the ocean: We listed Fish, Whale, Shark, Octopus, and Sea turtle. These animals are adapted to live in saltwater and have features for swimming, like fins or streamlined bodies. In the forest: We listed Lion, Tiger, Deer, Monkey, and Elephant. Forests have many trees and provide shelter and food for a variety of animals. In a pond: We listed Lotus, Tadpole, Duck, Water beetle, and Frog. These are adapted to freshwater environments. Lotus plants have leaves that float. Ducks have webbed feet for swimming. This shows that biodiversity varies greatly from region to region because the environmental conditions (like temperature, water availability, type of land) are different, and plants and animals have special features (adaptations) to survive in their specific ha you bend the stem easily, or is it stiff? Take care that the stems do not break.

items.stem: Lemon Plant Medium Brown (older parts), Green (younger parts) Hard Medium Thick Close to the ground Shrub
items.answer: During our nature walk, we observed different plants. The mango tree was much taller than us. Its stem was brown, very hard, and thick. The branches started higher up on the stem. So, it is a Tree. The rose plant was about my height (medium). Its stem was brown, hard, but thin. It had many branches starting close to the ground. So, it is a Shrub. The tomato plant was shorter than me. Its stem was green, tender (soft), and thin. Its branches also appeared close to the ground. So, it is a Herb. We also looked at grass. It was very short, with green, tender, and thin stems. It is also a Herb. A lemon plant we saw was medium height. Its older stems were brownish and hard, while newer stems were green and a bit softer. The stem was of medium thickness, and branches started near the ground. So, it is a Shrub. items.stem: As the population grows and people want more comfortable lives, forests are being cut down to meet various needs. How can this affect our surroundings? How do you think we can address this challenge?
items.answer: Cutting forests removes the homes of many plants and animals, reduces rainfall, causes soil to wash away, and increases the amount of carbon dioxide in the air, making Earth warmer. We can plant more trees (afforestation), save paper and wood, use recycled or alternative materials, support laws that protect forests, and spread awareness so everyone understands why trees are important.

items.answer: A (reticulate venation examples): Hibiscus, Mango, Pea. B (parallel venation examples): Wheat, Rice, Maize.

items.stem: Observe the labelled part of a duck in the picture below. What differences do you observe in the feet of the duck compared to the other birds? Which activity would the duck be able to perform using this part?
items.answer: The duck’s feet are webbed—a thin skin stretches between its toes, making each foot look like a paddle. In birds such as the pigeon, the toes are separate and end in claws for perching. Because of its webbed feet, the duck can swim efficiently; the broad surface pushes against water just like oars, helping the bird move smoothly in ponds and lakes.

items.stem: What is biodiversity?

options.label: A
options.text: The study of a single species in a specific area

options.label: B
options.text: The variety of plants and animals found in a particular region

options.label: C
options.text: The total number of animals in an ecosystem

options.label: D
options.text: The interaction between plants and their environment

items.answer: (B) The variety of plants and animals found in a particular region. Biodiversity refers to the wide range of plant and animal life present in a specific habitat or geographical area. This variety contributes to the overall health and balance of the ecosystem.

items.stem: What did Dr. Raghu advise the students to notice during the nature walk, emphasizing respect for living creatures?

options.label: A
options.text: Only the different types of trees

options.label: B
options.text: The variety of smells and to observe without disturbing

options.label: C
options.text: The colors of the flowers exclusively

options.label: D
options.text: The number of insects they could find

items.answer: (B) The variety of smells and to observe without disturbing. Dr. Raghu advised the students to notice the variety of smells in the park and emphasized respecting all living creatures by observing them without causing any disturbance during their nature walk.

items.stem: Why is grouping plants and animals important in science?

options.label: A
options.text: It makes it harder to study individual species

options.label: B
options.text: It primarily helps in naming new organisms

options.label: C
options.text: It makes it easier to understand and study them based on similarities and differences

options.label: D
options.text: It is only useful for creating museum exhibits

items.answer: (C) It makes it easier to understand and study them based on similarities and differences. Grouping organisms based on shared characteristics (similarities) and distinguishing features (differences) helps in organizing the vast diversity of life, making it more manageable to study and understand relationships between different organisms.

items.stem: What are plants with soft, green, and tender stems, typically small in size, called?

options.label: A
options.text: Trees

options.label: B
options.text: Shrubs

options.label: C
options.text: Herbs

options.label: D
options.text: Creepers

items.answer: (C) Herbs Herbs are characterized by their relatively small size and stems that are soft, green, and tender. Tomato plants are an example of herbs.

items.stem: Which of the following plants is an example of a shrub?

options.label: A
options.text: Mango tree

options.label: B
options.text: Tomato plant

options.label: C
options.text: Rose plant

options.label: D
options.text: Common grass

items.answer: (C) Rose plant The shrubs as plants that are not as tall as trees, often with many brown woody stems branching near the ground. A rose plant is cited as an example.

items.stem: What is the primary basis for classifying plants into herbs, shrubs, and trees?

options.label: A
options.text: The color and shape of their flowers

options.label: B
options.text: The height and nature of their stems

options.label: C
options.text: The type of fruits they produce

options.label: D
options.text: The environment in which they grow

items.answer: (B) The height and nature of their stems. On observing plant height and stem characteristics (like hardness, thickness, and branching patterns) to group them into herbs, shrubs, or trees.

items.stem: What is venation in leaves?

options.label: A
options.text: The color pattern on the leaf surface

options.label: B
options.text: The texture of the leaf

options.label: C
options.text: The pattern of veins on the leaf

options.label: D
options.text: The way leaves are attached to the stem

items.answer: (C) The pattern of veins on the leaf. Venation refers to the arrangement or pattern of veins, which are thin lines visible on the surface of a leaf. These veins are crucial for transporting water and nutrients.

items.stem: What is the main difference between reticulate venation and parallel venation in leaves?

options.label: A
options.text: Reticulate venation has veins parallel to each other, while parallel venation has a net-like pattern

options.label: B
options.text: Reticulate venation is found in grasses, while parallel venation is found in hibiscus

options.label: C
options.text: Reticulate venation forms a net-like pattern, while parallel venation has veins running parallel

options.label: D
options.text: Reticulate venation refers to thick veins, while parallel venation refers to thin veins

items.answer: (C) Reticulate venation forms a net-like pattern, while parallel venation has veins running parallel. Reticulate venation is characterized by a web- like or net-like arrangement of veins, as seen in hibiscus leaves. Parallel venation features veins that run parallel to one another, typical of banana or grass leaves.

items.stem: What type of root system consists of one main root with smaller side roots arising from it?

options.label: A
options.text: Fibrous root system

options.label: B
options.text: Taproot system

options.label: C
options.text: Adventitious root system

options.label: D
options.text: Prop root system

items.answer: (B) Taproot system A taproot system is characterized by a prominent, central main root (the taproot) from which smaller, lateral roots branch out. The mustard plant is an example of this.

items.stem: Which type of root system is generally found in common grass plants?

options.label: A
options.text: Taproot system

options.label: B
options.text: Fibrous root system

options.label: C
options.text: Prop root system

options.label: D
options.text: Stilt root system

items.answer: (B) Fibrous root system Common grass plants typically have a fibrous root system, where a bunch of similar-sized, thin roots arise from the base of the stem, rather than having a single main root.

items.stem: What general relationship is observed between leaf venation and the type of root system in plants?

options.label: A
options.text: Plants with reticulate venation usually have fibrous roots

options.label: B
options.text: Plants with parallel venation usually have taproots

options.label: C
options.text: Plants with reticulate venation usually have taproots, and those with parallel venation usually have fibrous roots

options.label: D
options.text: There is no general relationship between leaf venation and root type

items.answer: (C) Plants with reticulate venation usually have taproots, and those with parallel venation usually have fibrous roots. There is a general pattern where plants with reticulate (net-like) venation usually have taproots, while those with parallel venation typically have fibrous root systems.

items.stem: What are cotyledons?

options.label: A
options.text: The first leaves that emerge from a seed

options.label: B
options.text: The protective outer covering of a seed

options.label: C
options.text: The parts of a seed that can sometimes be split, like in a chickpea

options.label: D
options.text: The small roots that develop from a germinating seed

items.answer: (C) The parts of a seed that can sometimes be split, like in a chickpea. Cotyledons are embryonic leaves within a seed. In dicotyledonous plants like chickpeas, the seed can be split into two such parts. They often store food for the embryo.

items.stem: How many cotyledons does a maize seed typically have?

options.label: A
options.text: Two

options.label: B
options.text: One

options.label: C
options.text: Three

options.label: D
options.text: None

items.answer: (B) One (single thin cotyledon) Maize is an example of a monocotyledonous plant, meaning its seeds contain a single, often thin, cotyledon.

items.stem: What are the typical characteristics of dicot plants regarding their leaf venation and root system?

options.label: A
options.text: Parallel venation and fibrous root system

options.label: B
options.text: Reticulate venation and fibrous root system

options.label: C
options.text: Parallel venation and taproot system

options.label: D
options.text: Reticulate venation and taproot system

items.answer: (D) Reticulate venation and taproot system. Dicotyledonous (dicot) plants generally exhibit reticulate venation in their leaves and possess a taproot system, where there’s a main central root.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a main feature used to classify animals?

options.label: A
options.text: The type of movement they exhibit

options.label: B
options.text: The body parts they use for movement

options.label: C
options.text: The sounds they make

options.label: D
options.text: Where they live (their habitat)

items.answer: (C) The sounds they make. Although bird chirps are mentioned as an example of diversity, animals are mainly grouped based on how they move, the body parts they use for movement, and their habitats not primarily by the sounds they make.

items.stem: How would you categorize the fact that a fish uses its fins to swim in water?

options.label: A
options.text: Type of food and habitat

options.label: B
options.text: Type of movement and body parts used for movement

options.label: C
options.text: Color and size of the animal

options.label: D
options.text: Reproductive method and lifespan

items.answer: (B) Type of movement and body parts used for movement. The statement “a fish uses its fins to swim in water” relates directly to how the animal moves (swimming) and which body parts it uses for that movement (fins). This fits under the category of type of movement and body parts used for movement, making option (B) the correct choice.

items.stem: What are adaptations?

options.label: A
options.text: The scientific names given to plants and animals

options.label: B
options.text: The general behaviors common to all living organisms

options.label: C
options.text: Special features that enable plants and animals to survive in a particular region

options.label: D
options.text: The diseases that affect plants and animals in specific habitats

items.answer: (C) Special features that enable plants and animals to survive in a particular region. Adaptations are specific physical or behavioral characteristics that have evolved in organisms, allowing them to live successfully and reproduce in their particular environment or habitat.

items.stem: Which of the following is an example of a terrestrial habitat?

options.label: A
options.text: Ponds

options.label: B
options.text: Oceans

options.label: C
options.text: Forests

options.label: D
options.text: Rivers

items.answer: (C) Forests Terrestrial habitats are defined as places where plants and animals live on land, with forests given as one example of this type of habitat.

items.stem: Why does the biodiversity of a hot desert differ significantly from that of a cold mountainous region?

options.label: A
options.text: Because animals in deserts are always larger

options.label: B
options.text: Because plants in mountains do not need water

options.label: C
options.text: Because plants and animals have different adaptations to survive the distinct environmental conditions

options.label: D
options.text: Because all species prefer mountainous regions for their beauty

items.answer: (C) Because plants and animals have different adaptations to survive the distinct environmental conditions. Different regions have vastly different environmental conditions (e.g., temperature, water availability). Organisms living in these regions possess specific adaptations (special features) that help them survive those particular conditions, leading to diverse forms of life.

items.stem: What is a habitat?

options.label: A
options.text: The food that an animal eats

options.label: B
options.text: The place where plants and animals live

options.label: C
options.text: The way an animal moves

options.label: D
options.text: The group to which a plant belongs

items.answer: (B) The place where plants and animals live. A habitat is the natural environment or home of a plant, animal, or other organism. It provides the resources necessary for survival, such as food, water, and shelter.

items.stem: What unique feature helps deodar trees survive in snowy mountainous regions?

options.label: A
options.text: They have very deep root systems

options.label: B
options.text: They produce brightly colored flowers to attract pollinators

options.label: C
options.text: Their conical shape and sloping branches allow snow to slide off easily

options.label: D
options.text: Their leaves are very thick and store a lot of water

items.answer: (C) Their conical shape and sloping branches allow snow to slide off easily. Deodar trees, found in mountainous regions with snowfall, have a conical shape and flexible, sloping branches. This structure is an adaptation that helps prevent snow accumulation, allowing them to survive such conditions.

items.stem: How does the damage to habitats lead to a loss of biodiversity?

options.label: A
options.text: It forces animals to learn new ways of finding food

options.label: B
options.text: It results in the loss of homes, food, and other resources for plants and animals

options.label: C
options.text: It primarily affects only the plant populations

options.label: D
options.text: It causes animals to migrate to more populated areas

items.answer: (B) It results in the loss of homes, food, and other resources for plants and animals. When habitats are damaged or destroyed, the plants and animals that depend on those habitats for survival lose their homes, food sources, and other essential resources, which can lead to a decline in their populations and ultimately, a loss of biodiversity.

items.stem: What was the name of the movement that began in the early 1970s in Uttarakhand to stop the cutting of trees?

options.label: A
options.text: Save Silent Valley movement

options.label: B
options.text: Project Tiger

options.label: C
options.text: Chipko movement

options.label: D
options.text: Green India Mission

items.answer: (C) Chipko movement The Chipko movement, which began in the early 1970s in Uttarakhand, was a significant environmental movement where local people, especially women, hugged trees to protect them from being felled, thus saving forests.

items.stem: What are sacred groves ?

options.label: A
options.text: Gardens specifically designed for growing medicinal plants

options.label: B
options.text: Man-made forests planted for commercial purposes

options.label: C
options.text: Undisturbed patches of forests protected by local communities

options.label: D
options.text: Areas designated for scientific research on trees

items.answer: (C) Undisturbed patches of forests protected by local communities. Sacred groves are traditionally protected patches of forest that are preserved by local communities, often due to religious or cultural beliefs. These areas harbor rich biodiversity because human interference is typically restricted.

items.stem: Who is referred to as the ‘Birdman of India’?

items.stem: Which of the following is an example that illustrates the interdependence between plants and animals?

options.label: A
options.text: Trees competing for sunlight

options.label: B
options.text: Animals helping in spreading seeds after eating fruits

options.label: C
options.text: Birds building nests on trees without benefiting the tree

options.label: D
options.text: Different animal species competing for the same food source

items.answer: (B) Animals helping in spreading seeds after eating fruits. When animals consume fruits and then disperse the seeds through their droppings, they help in the propagation of plants. This is a clear example of the mutual dependence between plants and animals.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a tree?

options.label: A
options.text: Grows really tall

options.label: B
options.text: Has soft, green, and tender stems

options.label: C
options.text: Has hard, thick, brown, and woody stems

options.label: D
options.text: Branches typically start higher up on the stem

items.answer: (B) Has soft, green, and tender stems. Trees are characterized by their height, and hard, thick, woody stems. Soft, green, and tender stems are characteristic of herbs, not trees.

items.stem: How do climbers and creepers differ in their growth habit?

options.label: A
options.text: Climbers grow tall independently, while creepers need support

options.label: B
options.text: Climbers creep along the ground, while creepers need support to climb

options.label: C
options.text: Climbers need support to climb and grow, while creepers spread along the ground

options.label: D
options.text: Both climbers and creepers have very strong, woody stems

items.answer: (C) Climbers need support to climb and grow, while creepers spread along the ground. Plants with weak stems that use external support to grow upwards are called climbers. Plants that spread out horizontally along the ground are known as creepers.

items.stem: A student observes a plant with leaves showing a net-like pattern of veins. Based on the information, what type of root system is this plant most likely to have?

options.text: Fibrous root system

options.label: B
options.text: Taproot system

options.label: C
options.text: Adventitious roots

options.label: D
options.text: No root system

items.answer: (B) Taproot system It is generally observed that plants with reticulate (net-like) venation in their leaves, such as the rose (a dicot), usually have a taproot system—showing a common pattern in plant structure.

items.stem: Assertion (A) : Camels found in hot deserts excrete small amounts of urine and have dry dung. Reason (R) : These features are adaptations to conserve water in arid environments.

options.label: A
options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: B
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: C
options.text: A is true, but R is false

options.label: D
options.text: A is false, but R is true

items.answer: (A) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. Camels in hot deserts producing concentrated urine and dry dung are crucial adaptations. These mechanisms minimize water loss, which is essential for survival in environments where water is scarce.

items.stem: Damage to habitats does not affect biodiversity. Which of the above statements is/are correct?

options.label: A
options.text: 1 only

options.label: B
options.text: 2 only

options.label: C
options.text: 1 and 3 only

options.label: D
options.text: 2 and 3 only

items.answer: (B) 2 only Biodiversity includes the variety of both plants and animals. Each organism plays a role in its ecosystem. Habitat damage directly leads to loss of biodiversity. Therefore, only statement 2 is correct.

items.stem: During a nature walk, students are asked to group plants based on their stem characteristics. One plant is observed to be medium height with several hard, brown, woody stems branching out near the ground. Into which group would this plant most likely be classified?

options.label: A
options.text: Herb

options.label: B
options.text: Shrub
